1:
Every voice takes the messenger for John the Baptist, each for a different reason. Gill clears away the alternatives proposed by Jewish commentators, the angel of death, an angel from heaven, and Malachi himself, and argues from the sending: the title belongs to John not by nature but by office, and he is Christ's messenger because sent by him, which shows Christ's authority in sending ministers and his existence before the man he sent. Ellicott works from the Hebrew, which is the prophet's own name, and thinks he was doubtless influenced in his choice of term by it; from the nature of the mission he identifies this figure with the Elijah promised in the next chapter. Clarke supplies the picture, the custom of sending pioneers ahead of an eastern monarch's march. Henry reads the verse as a direct answer to the atheistical demand closing the previous chapter, where is the God of judgment: here he is, just at the door; and he observes that the gospel opens by claiming this promise fulfilled, so that the two Testaments are tacked together and made to answer one another.

Who the Lord is that comes to his temple Ellicott settles philologically. The word occurs eight times with the definite article and everywhere else has the name of God following it; here it can only mean God himself, since he comes to his own temple and is the one they seek, the God of judgment they had just demanded. The messenger of the covenant, he notes, is found nowhere else in Scripture, and since the figure is identified with the Lord he can be no other than the Son of God manifested in the flesh; he would render the last clause desire rather than delight in. Wesley identifies the building as the second temple lately built by Zerubbabel and Joshua, and reads the closing clause with an edge, that few of that people did not please themselves with the thought of his coming, though from various motives.

Calvin sets the whole against the slanders that provoked it. The prophet does not comfort the scoffers but asserts his own faith against them, as though to say that though they declare themselves deceived or forsaken by the God they hoped in, his covenant shall not be in vain; God triumphs over them by alleging that covenant, since their murmurings could not hinder him from performing in due time what they thought would never be done. He also finds an allusion to Moses in the sending of a forerunner, since God's majesty was then more than the people could bear without an intercessor, so that they cried out for someone to speak to them lest they die. He adds that Christ himself so explains the passage, than whom no better interpreter can be found.

On who can abide that day, the answers turn on who is judged. Keil and Delitzsch is most explicit: the judgment that begins with the coming is not upon the heathen, for which the ungodly nation was longing, but upon the godless within the covenant nation, and the question itself has a negative force, that no one endures it. Gill fills in what could not be borne: the doctrine of Christ's deity and equality with the Father, of a kingdom spiritual and not temporal, and of a grace that struck at the self-righteous principles of the Scribes and Pharisees. Ellicott makes the coming a crucial test, and says the people ought to have considered how far they were prepared for the advent before desiring it so eagerly. Clarke answers that only those who believe on his name may abide it, and notes of the second figure that the word comes from a root meaning to cleanse and covers anything that deterges, such as fern ashes, since he doubts whether the composition we call soap was known in ancient times.
3:
The figure of the refiner is worked at different levels. Clarke keeps to the craft, picturing a refiner of metals sitting at his fire, increasing it when he sees necessary and watching the process of his work. Gill reports a Jewish commentator who makes the day rather than the Lord the refiner, comparing it to a judge who separates the guilty from the innocent, but takes it of the Lord himself, whose diligence in separating good men and principles from bad is what the sitting expresses; and he notes that one Jewish authority understood the passage of the Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch renders the verse with the trade terms throughout, a smelter sitting to purify and refine the children of Levi so that they may offer their sacrifice in righteousness.

Who the sons of Levi are, and what they offer, is where the readings part. Clarke takes them for those who minister in their stead under the new covenant, the old Levitical institutions being abolished; a great number of the priests did become obedient to the faith under the preaching of Christ, and the rest this great Refiner threw as dross into the fire that consumed Jerusalem and the temple. Ellicott keeps them the priests of the prophet's own day, on the principle that judgment must begin at the house of God, and adds two qualifications: the phrase about righteousness refers to the moral character of the offerer rather than the kind of sacrifice, and neither this verse nor the next implies material sacrifices in Messianic times, the prophet speaking in language suitable to his own age. On the days of old he will define the period only tentatively, from the time of Moses to the first year of Solomon's reign, and adds that it seems characteristic of this prophet to be somewhat a praiser of times past.

The catalogue of offences that follows is treated as a list of breaches of the law. Ellicott takes each in turn, sorcery, adultery, false swearing, the withholding of wages, the oppression of widow and orphan, and injustice to a stranger, and shows every one explicitly forbidden already. Clarke gives the same list with more feeling, calling it a horrible crew and observing that the land was then full of them, though several were converted under the preaching of Christ. Gill fixes the coming historically, not at the last day but at the destruction of Jerusalem, and turns the scoffers' question against them: there will be no need to inquire after him, for when he comes he will be near enough, and too near for them.

The declaration that God does not change is read as the ground of the nation's survival. Ellicott would render it simply that Jehovah changes not, and draws the inference: because it is the Eternal's unchangeable will that the sons of Jacob should not perish as a nation, he will purify them by eradicating the wicked among them, so that the remnant may return to their allegiance. He reports another scholar's rendering, which makes the clause say that the Lord has not changed but asks whether the sons of Jacob have not altered, and rejects it on two grounds, that the verb does not mean to alter and that the received sense agrees exactly with the wording of a prayer in Ezra. Clarke draws the same point for the new dispensation, which is not the effect of any change in God's counsels but the fulfilment of his everlasting purposes, as is the laying aside of the Mosaic ritual; and it is because of the ancient covenant, he says, that the nation is preserved distinct, a monument of justice and mercy. Keil and Delitzsch reads the verse as the hinge of the argument, where God, having announced that he will draw near in judgment, turns to explain why he has hitherto withheld his blessing.
7:
The charge opens as a general one before it is made specific. Gill treats the verse as the head of an enumeration of the sins that were the cause of the nation's ruin, and takes the first count to be apostasy from the statutes and ordinances of the law, which they made void by the traditions of the fathers; the phrase about their fathers he reads as pointing both to that evil and to an early, long and continued departure. Ellicott reads it more sweepingly still, that throughout the whole course of their history they had been such a people, and that when they are now exhorted to repent they ask in feigned innocence what there is to return from. Clarke puts the same fault as a failure of spirit rather than of letter, that they never acted according to the design of the ordinances; and he explains their question by their consciences, which were so seared that they did not know themselves to be sinners.

Henry runs the whole passage on a single figure. This is God's controversy with that generation for deserting his service and robbing him, and they are wicked servants indeed who not only run away from their Master but run away with their Master's goods. The ordinances of worship were the business they were to mind, the talents they were to trade with, and the trust committed to them to keep; and they went away from them, grew weary of them, withdrew the neck from that yoke, deviated from the rule prescribed them and betrayed what was lodged with them. On the phrase about the fathers he offers two senses, either that the disobedience runs back to the fathers of old who were sent into captivity for it, or that in the few generations since the return the people have fallen off from what they were when they first came back; and he notes that the confession of the same trespass stands in the record of that return.

That God can be robbed at all is what the next charge turns on. Gill notes that the word may also be read of the gods of the nations, and observes the sting in that reading, since the heathen would not do such a thing, accounting sacrilege a great sin, and yet this the people were guilty of; the Targum, he adds, takes it of judges rather than of gods. Ellicott explains why withholding from the Levites counts as robbing God: the tithes are first offered to Jehovah, and it is he who then gives them to the Levites in the place of an inheritance. Clarke states the consequence plainly, that by withholding the tithes and offerings from the temple they left the divine worship neglected.

The curse pronounced on the whole nation is understood of the harvest. Gill notes that one old version renders the word penury, which he grants is not a proper rendering but says gives the true sense of the curse they lay under, since rain was withheld from them for their sins and the earth did not bring forth its usual increase, so that there was want of food in all their land and their blessings themselves were cursed. Clarke states it as a verdict on the whole people, that the nation is under God's displeasure. Ellicott simply refers the reader back to the curse on the blessings pronounced in the previous chapter and forward to the promise of relief that follows, so that the sentence here stands between the two.
10:
The command about the tithes is explained by what the storehouse was. Gill describes the arrangement in some detail: there were places in the temple where the tithe was put and from which it was distributed to the priests and Levites as their families needed, and he distinguishes the several tithes, the tenth of all eatable things paid to the Levites, the tithe taken out of that tithe and paid by the Levites to the priests, and a further tithe which in some years the owners ate themselves at Jerusalem and in others gave to the poor. Ellicott adds the history of the building, that from the time of Hezekiah there were special storehouses at the sanctuary for the purpose and again in the second temple, and points out that the emphasis of the command falls on the word all. Clarke states the emergency that lay behind it, that the withholding had gone so far that the priests had not food enough to support life and the sacred service was interrupted.

The promise attached to the command is the only place in the prophets where God invites a trial of himself, and each voice handles it differently. Clarke turns it into a maxim, that what is given to God shall never lessen a man's store, and paraphrases the challenge: give as you should, and see whether the windows of heaven are not so opened, with rain and fruitful seasons, that your barns and granaries cannot contain the abundance. Ellicott looks for a case already on record and finds one in the chronicle of Hezekiah's reform, where the chief priest reports that since the people began to bring in the offerings there has been enough to eat and plenty left over. On the closing clause he prefers to render the conjunction until rather than that, keeps the received sense that there shall not be room enough to receive the blessing, and declines a rendering proposed by one lexicographer which would make it say until the divine abundance is exhausted, as a way of saying for ever. Keil and Delitzsch renders the same clause as a pouring out to superabundance.

The rebuke of the devourer is read as a promise of ordinary providence rather than of miracle. Gill takes the devourer for the locust or caterpillar or any such creature that eats up the herbage and the fruit of trees, and observes that every such creature is under the restraint of providence, so that by a nod they are prevented from doing the mischief they otherwise would, being the Lord's great army which he can send and call off as he pleases. Clarke divides the promise in two, that the locusts shall not come on the crops and that those already in the country shall be dispersed and destroyed, and reads the second half as a guarantee that every blossom shall bear fruit and every bunch of grapes come to maturity. Ellicott notices that the phrase rendered for your sakes is the same word used in the previous chapter of the threat against the priests, there in a bad sense and here in a good, and would render the verb corrupt rather than rebuke. Keil and Delitzsch renders the promise about the vine as a miscarrying, that it will not miscarry in the field, and closes the passage with the nations calling the people blessed and the land itself a land of good pleasure. Gill takes the praise of the nations as following on what they will see, a land freed from the devouring locust, the rains given in their season and the earth yielding a large increase.
13:
The charge of stout words is taken as a formal indictment. Henry calls it exactly that, an indictment for treasonable words spoken against the King of kings, and traces the stoutness to pride, haughtiness and contempt of God; he supposes there was a club of them in league against religion, men who set up for wits and set their wits to work to ridicule it, strengthening one another's hands. Gill describes the speech as hard and strong, bearing very hardly upon God, murmuring at his providence, arraigning his justice and despising his ordinances; he adds that one Jewish commentator took the passage for a prophecy of the times of the Messiah. Clarke says the address is to open infidels and revilers, who when challenged are ready either to deny the whole or impudently to maintain what they had said. Ellicott alone reads the opening clause differently, rendering it that their words put a constraint on God, namely to prove himself to them the God of judgment they had demanded; and he prefers conversed together to spoken, taking them to have been in the habit of comparing the promises made to them with the state of affairs as they found it.

Henry pauses over the mixture in the nation. Though all at that time enjoyed the same privileges and advantages there were men of very different characters among them, as there ever were and ever will be in the world and in the church, like the good and the bad figs of the older prophet, tares and wheat in the same field, chaff and corn on the same floor; and what follows is an account of both sorts.

The complaint that service is vain is understood as an argument from experience. Gill takes it as said in their hearts if not with their lips, that a man gets nothing by serving God, has no reward, and fares no better than the wicked, indeed worse; and he reports another Jewish commentator who turns it round to the other party, so that worship is said to be no way profitable to God either, nor regarded by him, and is therefore vain since neither he nor they are the better for it. Clarke makes it a settled teaching rather than a mood, that they asserted men should be nothing the better for worship and nothing the worse for neglecting it, and declared even repentance useless, and that this was what they taught the people. Ellicott stays with the last clause and identifies the practice complained of, that walking mournfully means with all the outward signs of fasting, and that the fasts meant are voluntary ones rather than the appointed day; and he finds in the complaint, already in a somewhat developed form, that disposition to attribute merit to outward observances for their own sake, without regard to the secret attitude of the heart, which reached its height in a later generation.

Calling the proud happy is where the three readings converge. Gill glosses the word as meaning presumptuous sinners who stretch out their hands against God, and sets the picture side by side: these enjoy all worldly happiness while those who serve the Lord are mourning in sackcloth. Clarke states it as a general observation and half concedes it, that proud and insolent men domineer everywhere and none dares resist them, that the humble and holy are depressed while the proud and wicked hold the places of trust and profit, and that too often it is so; even those who insult God's justice, he adds, are preserved from dangers while the righteous fall by them. Ellicott locates the grievance more precisely, in a promise unfulfilled: God had said they should be a proverb among the nations for blessedness, and seeing things as they are they feel more inclined to give that name to the proud instead.
16:
Who it is that speaks to one another here is not quite settled. Gill reports a Jewish commentator who continues the speech of the wicked here, taking the verb so that those who feared God were destroyed one with another, particularly by plague, while the workers of wickedness were set up; but Gill takes the verse as set against what the scoffers said, spoken by those who at that time feared the Lord and embraced the Messiah. He adds a definition of the fear meant, which takes in the whole of religious worship, and describes not those who dread God's wrath but those who have a filial and holy fear, a reverential affection for him. Clarke fills in the circumstances: there were a few godly in the land who, hearing the language and seeing the profligacy of the rebels, concluded that some signal mark of God's vengeance must fall upon them, and who cleaved the closer to their Maker as the corruption increased. He finds three marks of them, that they feared the Lord with a reverence that made them depart from evil, that they spake often one to another and so kept up the communion of saints, and that they thought on his name, which was to them a fruitful source of edifying meditation, the name of God being God himself in the plenitude of his power, justice, goodness and truth.

The book written before God is explained from court practice. Clarke has the Lord hearkening to their conversation and hearing the meditations of their hearts, and approving the whole so far that their names were registered in heaven; he finds behind the image an allusion to the records kept by kings of those who had performed signal services and were to be first rewarded.

The word rendered jewels draws a flat objection. Clarke will not have it: the term means a peculium, a proper treasure, that which is a man's own and most prized by him, and nowhere in the Bible does it mean a gem or precious stone, so that the interpretations commonly given, comparing the saints to jewels, are forced and false. Ellicott reaches the same result by translation, rendering the clause that they shall be to God a special possession on the day that he is about to make. Gill dwells on the claim itself: they are Christ's already by his Father's gift, by his own purchase, by the conquests of his grace and by their voluntary surrender of themselves, but in that day they will be claimed and owned before his Father and the holy angels. Clarke reads the sparing as a father's act, God taking care of them when he comes to visit the wicked, and acting towards them as a tender father acts towards his most loving and obedient son.

The last verse turns on who returns and to what. Gill offers both, either the wicked, who as some render the word will be converted and change their minds, or those who feared the Lord, who will have a clearer discerning of persons and of the dispensations of providence; he reports a commentator who refers the returning to the resurrection and to souls returning to their bodies, but himself refers the whole to Christ's first coming and the destruction of Jerusalem. Clarke has the scoffers returning to their senses, perhaps too late, and seeing the difference God makes between the obedience they called unprofitable and the disobedience they called harmless. Wesley says the same more briefly, that they are forced back to their reason by the convincing power of God's judgments. Ellicott presses the word again, rendering the clause that they shall once more perceive the difference, and points out that God had made such a difference manifest before, as between the Egyptians and the Israelites in the matter of the darkness.
